designPrinciple: Asymmetric balance: factions begin with different strengths, constraints and theatres. No faction receives hidden combat bonuses merely to equalise outcomes.

factions.name: United States
startingStrengths: advanced air, naval, space and intelligence capabilities
substantial domestic energy and agricultural capacity
startingPressures: simultaneous commitments in Greenland, Europe and the Middle East
hostile or uncertain access to allied bases and supply routes
strategic ambiguity toward China, Russia and North Korea
political and economic costs of sustaining several distant theatres
factions.balanceIntent: Powerful enough to survive temporary isolation, but unable to dominate every theatre without prioritising, negotiating or rebuilding access relationships.

factions.name: European Defence Coalition
startingStrengths: strong defensive motivation in Europe and the North Atlantic
startingPressures: two-front war against the United States and Russia
member-state political constraints and uneven mobilisation
dependence on intact shipping, undersea cables and cross-border logistics
factions.balanceIntent: Potentially the largest aggregate bloc, but its power should depend on coalition cohesion, logistics and successful substitution rather than appearing instantly as one perfectly integrated state.

factions.name: Eurasian Accommodation
startingStrengths: large resource and industrial bases in aggregate
ability to trade and coordinate without formal military integration
several nearby neutral or non-aligned states available for diplomacy and commerce
startingPressures: different strategic objectives and mutual distrust
exposure to maritime interdiction and sanctions in some sectors
risk that opportunistic expansion provokes balancing coalitions
factions.balanceIntent: Less integrated than the other camps, but able to exploit local superiority, trade networks and opponents' distraction. Cooperation should remain contingent rather than guaranteed.

antiSnowballRules: occupation creates garrison, legitimacy and logistics costs
long supply lines reduce effective military power
coalition members can limit access, basing and war participation
sanctions and blockades create substitution and smuggling incentives rather than binary shutdowns
heavy casualties and infrastructure loss increase domestic pressure for de-escalation
rapid territorial expansion raises balancing pressure among nearby uncommitted powers
